title: The spare on the shelf
bodyMd:
A fictional workshop reduced its stock of spare parts to release money tied up in inventory. For several months, the change appeared successful: storage costs fell and machines rarely stopped. Then a small inexpensive valve failed, and a replacement took two weeks to arrive. The machine it controlled remained unavailable throughout that period.

The manager did not restore every former stock item. Instead, the workshop classified parts by the consequences of failure, delivery time and the possibility of temporary substitution. A cheap part could justify a spare if its absence disabled valuable equipment, while an expensive part available locally within an hour might not. Inventory planning became less a question of keeping many or few objects and more a question of which interruptions the workshop was prepared to absorb.
